meta.title: Contribute: issues, pull requests and new agents
meta.description: Build ai-memory from source, pass the five required gates, find the right crate and open a pull request that merges on the first review. Rust, MIT licensed.

hero.title: Contribute to ai-memory
hero.lede: {n} people have landed code so far. This page gets you from an idea to the right issue, the right crate and a pull request that passes review the first time.

numbers.title: An active project, in numbers
numbers.lede: Counts come from the GitHub API when this site is built.

ways.title: Pick your way in
ways.lede: Each of these goes to the exact page on GitHub.

bug.title: Report a bug
bug.text: The template asks for your version, OS, agent, transport and the relevant server log lines.

feature.title: Propose a feature
feature.text: Proposals are issues; the repository has no discussions board. The template asks what problem it solves and whether it would break existing installs.

firstIssue.title: Find a first issue
firstIssue.text: The good first issue label marks work that suits a newcomer. Help wanted marks the rest.

harness.title: Add or fix a harness
harness.text: Managed harness support has a written protocol: prove the native session contract, read stores read-only, deliver context before acknowledging it, and ship the required tests.

docs.title: Improve the docs
docs.text: Guides live in docs/ as markdown. A doc fix is a normal pull request and skips the changelog when nothing user-facing changes.

companion.title: Build around it
companion.text: Importers, richer UIs and chat front ends belong in companion projects that use the public HTTP and MCP surfaces.

security.title: Security reports never go in a public issue
security.text: Open a private security advisory instead. SECURITY.md explains what to include and what to do if you cannot use GitHub’s advisory flow.

figure.alt: Diagram: a contribution moves through six stages, from an issue, to a branch, to the local gates, to a pull request, to review, and ships in the next release.
figure.caption: From idea to release. Fixes ship in the next patch, additive features in the next minor.

build.title: Get it building
build.lede: The build is self-contained. None of these commands needs an environment variable.

steps.title: Clone and build
steps.text: Rust 1.95 is required and pinned in rust-toolchain.toml, with rustfmt and clippy, so rustup installs the right toolchain on first build. SQLite is bundled and libgit2 is vendored. You need a standard C toolchain and nothing else.

steps.title: Use the everyday loop
steps.text: cargo t needs nextest: cargo install cargo-nextest --locked. It skips modules named slow or stress, which the pre-push hook and CI still run.

steps.title: Install the pre-push hook
steps.text: Once per clone. It only touches its own block in .git/hooks/pre-push. On a work-in-progress branch, git push --no-verify skips it.

steps.title: Pass the gates before you push
steps.text: CI enforces all five. Without nextest, cargo test --workspace --all-targets is the equivalent of cargo tf. If the last one is missing: cargo install cargo-deny cargo-audit.

steps.title: Check who your commits say you are
steps.text: Use an email verified on your GitHub account or its noreply address. History on main is never rewritten to fix attribution.

comments.allButSlow: all but the slow tier, ~20s warm
comments.oneCrate: one crate: builds only its test binaries
comments.oneTopic: one topic (builds everything, runs a subset)
comments.everyTest: every test (alias: cargo nextest run -P full)

rules.title: Ground rules and the acceptance bar
rules.lede: AGENTS.md is the canonical rules file for people and for coding agents. CONTRIBUTING.md condenses it to this.

landing.title: How work is expected to land

items.title: The changelog is a merge gate
items.text: Every user-facing change adds an entry under [Unreleased] in the same pull request. Reviewers treat a missing entry as blocking. Refactors and test-only changes are exempt.

items.title: Tests before “done”
items.text: Work counts as done once it has tests, above all parsers, ID derivation and the retention math.

items.title: No dead code, no half-built features
items.text: Stubs are documented in the module comment with the milestone that will finish them.

items.title: Stay inside the change
items.text: Do not refactor code the current milestone does not need.

items.title: Comments explain why
items.text: A comment that restates the line above it gets removed.

invariants.title: Invariants a pull request cannot break
items: All SQLite writes go through the single writer actor, WriterHandle.
Config is read once at startup. No std::env::var outside Config::load.
File writes are atomic: tmp, rename, fsync. Never in place.
Every wiki page is namespaced by (workspace_id, project_id).
The CLI is a thin HTTP client. It never opens the SQLite file or the wiki directory.
invariants.full: The full list, with the bug each one prevents, is in AGENTS.md

map.title: A map of the codebase
map.lede: Ten crates ship in the binary. Each has one responsibility and a typed API, and there are no circular dependencies.

figure.alt: Diagram: the crates in four tiers. The cli crate is on top. Below it are hooks, mcp, web, consolidate and workstream. Below those are store, wiki and llm. The core crate is the foundation under everything.
figure.caption: Crate names without the ai-memory- prefix. Everything depends on core, and only the cli crate depends on everything.

crates.core: Domain types, errors and ids. No IO.
crates.store: SQLite, the writer actor, the reader pool and the decay math.
crates.wiki: Atomic markdown writes, the file watcher and git.
crates.mcp: The MCP transport, the tool router and the admin routes.
crates.hooks: Hook payload schemas, the sanitizer and the /hook endpoint.
crates.llm: The provider auth boundary and the LLM and embedder traits.
crates.consolidate: Ingest, lint, sweep and the auto-improve pipeline.
crates.web: The read-only /web browser and the /api/v1 JSON routes.
crates.workstream: Read-only native transcript readers and the launch adapters behind ai-memory run.
crates.cli: The ai-memory binary and its thin HTTP subcommands.

dirs.companions: ai-memory-importer, a standalone package outside the root workspace. Build it with --manifest-path.
dirs.hooks: Lifecycle hook bundles, one folder per agent, shell and native.
dirs.evals: The benchmark harness. A workspace member that is never shipped.
dirs.docs: Architecture, design decisions, install, deploy and usage guides.
dirs.tests: End-to-end smoke tests, hook shell tests and fixtures.

map.tests: Integration tests live in tests/suite/ inside each crate. Helpers shared between crates go in crates/ai-memory-test-support, which is never shipped.

review.title: How pull requests get reviewed
review.lede: Reviews follow the pull request template, so filling it in honestly is most of the work.

items.title: The template is the checklist
items.text: It asks what changed, why, a test plan with the gates ticked, commit attribution, release impact and the changelog entry.

items.title: Say what kind of release it is
items.text: Tick patch, minor or major. A fix filed under “Added” can bump the wrong version, so put the changelog entry under the right heading.

items.title: Breaking changes wait for a major
items.text: Call them out in the description. They get the breaking-change label and are scheduled, so they do not hold up patch and minor releases.

items.title: CI is fast per merge
items.text: A merge gates on the fast Linux jobs. The macOS and Windows legs run on a label, nightly or by hand, and always before a release.

items.title: Fixes ship first
items.text: A bug fix goes out in the next patch release and is not held for feature work. A new harness or provider ships in the next minor.

review.harness: A harness pull request runs this shorter gate, records the CLI version it was tested against, and includes a manual pass against the real harness.
